title: Inherent holiness given with remission, not its meritorious cause
source_text: XV. Verum est quidem Deum neminem propter Christum a peccatis absolvere, quin simul illum induat habitu justitiae & sanctitatis verae, quae a primis initiis paulatim contendit ad perfectionem, ad quam demum in futuro saeculo perveniemus. Sed justitia illa licet Deo probetur, & promissionem habeat vitae & gloriae aeternae, nullo modo tamen causa est propter quam, & cujus merito a sempiterna poena peccatis nostris debita liberamur, & filii Dei per adoptionem, adeoque regni coelestis haeredes instituimur: Verum simul cum remissione peccatorum nostrorum justitiam ejusmodi propter Christi meritum & satisfactionem a Deo accipimus. Estque tam justitia ista quam remissio peccatorum respectu nostri mere gratuitum Dei donum. Neque haec ab illa tanquam a causa meritoria & impulsiva pendet.
pass_a_gloss: It is true that God absolves no one from sins for Christ’s sake without at the same time clothing him with a habit of true righteousness and holiness, which from first beginnings gradually presses on toward the perfection we shall at last reach in the age to come. But that righteousness, though it is approved by God and has the promise of eternal life and glory, is in no way the cause on account of which and by whose merit we are freed from the everlasting penalty due to our sins and are instituted sons of God by adoption and thus heirs of the heavenly kingdom. Rather, together with the remission of our sins we receive such righteousness from God on account of Christ’s merit and satisfaction. And both that righteousness and the remission of sins are, with respect to us, a merely gratuitous gift of God. Nor does the latter depend on the former as on a meritorious and impulsive cause.
pass_b_english: God never absolves without also clothing in true habitual holiness growing toward future perfection.
That inherent righteousness is not the meritorious cause of remission or adoption—both are free gifts for Christ’s sake.

choices.why: Denies inherent justice as meritorious of remission.
